personalExemptionScopingNote: Kansas SB1 (2024 special session) sets $9,160 single, $18,320 married filing jointly, and $2,320 per dependent. StatePersonalExemption (RetireSmartIRA/StatePersonalExemption.swift) has no dependent-count field, and a codebase grep found no dependent-count input anywhere in the app (no tax-dependents entry point exists at all). The Phase 5a Task 2 correction is therefore scoped to the single and married filing jointly amounts only; the $2,320 per-dependent amount is NOT modelled and is not folded into either base figure. None of the scenarios in this file describe a household with dependents, so no expectedStateTax value here is affected by this gap.

scenarios.name: Steve Nicolai's reported scenario: MFJ ordinary income, the missing SB1 personal exemption (defect 1 of 2, isolated, no pension involved)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 6, Form K-40 Line 4 instructions: 'If your filing status is married filing joint...enter 2 in the box for the number of exemptions and $18,320 in the amount box.' Same page, Kansas Standard Deduction table: Married Filing Joint $8,240 (matches this app's configured statetax-2026-KS.json stateDeduction.married). Per Senate Bill 1 (2024 Special Session), signed into law, ongoing for tax year 2024 and after (no sunset). Arithmetic reproducing Steve Nicolai's report to the cent: $50,000 income minus $8,240 MFJ standard deduction minus $18,320 MFJ personal exemption = $23,440 taxable. All of it falls in the first bracket (progressive schedule: 5.2% up to $46,000 MFJ threshold, 5.58% above). $23,440 x 5.2% = $1,218.88.

scenarios.name: single filer, ordinary income, the same missing personal exemption at a different income level and filing status (defect 1 of 2, isolated, no pension involved)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 6, Form K-40 Line 4 instructions: 'If your filing status is single, married filing separate or head of household...enter one in the box for number of exemptions and $9,160 in the amount box.' Same page, Kansas Standard Deduction table: Single $3,605. Arithmetic: $30,000 minus $3,605 single standard deduction minus $9,160 single personal exemption = $17,235 taxable, entirely inside the 5.2% first bracket (single threshold $23,000). $17,235 x 5.2% = $896.22.

scenarios.name: single filer, private pension: correctly fully taxable under KS law both ways; this case isolates that the only gap here is the shared personal-exemption defect above, not a per-source error (defect 2 of 2 contrast case)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14 'Retirement benefits specifically exempt from Kansas Income Tax' enumerates a closed list of Kansas public and federal plans, including Federal Civil Service Retirement/Disability Fund and U.S. Armed Forces retirement benefits (incl. Thrift Savings Plans), U.S. Railroad Retirement Board plans, KPERS annuities, Kansas Police and Firemen's Retirement System pensions, Overland Park Police/Fire Department retirement distributions, Kansas Teachers' Retirement annuities, Kansas Highway Patrol pensions, Kansas Justices and Judges Retirement System annuities, Board of Public Utilities pensions, Regents/faculty retirement annuity contracts, Washburn University retirement/pension benefits, and certain Kansas first-class-city pensions not covered by KPERS; a private-employer pension is on none of these enumerated categories and remains in federal AGI (fully taxable), same as under current KS law with no A14 subtraction available. Arithmetic (age 68, single): $40,000 minus $3,605 standard deduction minus $9,160 personal exemption = $27,235 taxable. $23,000 x 5.2% = $1,196.00, plus ($27,235-$23,000) x 5.58% = $4,235 x 5.58% = $236.313. Total $1,432.31.

scenarios.name: single filer, KPERS pension, same income as the private-pension case above: fully exempt under KS law, engine treats it identically to the private pension (defect 2 of 2, isolated by comparison)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14: 'Kansas Public Employees' Retirement (KPERS) annuities' is one entry on the closed list of Kansas public and federal plans enumerated as fully subtractable retirement benefits (the same list also includes Kansas Police and Firemen's, Teachers', Highway Patrol, Justices and Judges, Board of Public Utilities, Regents/Washburn University, and certain first-class-city plans -- see the private-pension case above for the full enumeration), with no dollar cap and no age gate stated for KPERS. KPERS is labelled 'ownStateOrLocal' here: the taxpayer's OWN state retirement system, which is exactly what KPERS is to a Kansas resident. Phase 5b Task 1 added that PlanSource case and Task 2 re-labelled this row onto it. Before those tasks the only available label was 'otherStateOrLocal' (doc-commented as 'a DIFFERENT state or its localities'), disclosed at the time as a stretch; that label was not merely imprecise, it was the exact case whose reason for existing is to STOP an out-of-state pension from claiming a state's own exclusion, so a Kansas rule written against it would have exempted a California pension too. The out-of-state guard case at the end of this file is what now proves it does not. Arithmetic: KPERS $40,000 is fully exempt under KS law, leaving $0 in state taxable income (before or after the standard deduction/personal exemption, which have nothing left to act on), so tax is $0.00. Comparing this case's engine figure to the private-pension case immediately above (both use the identical $40,000/age 68/single inputs) isolates exactly what the per-source rule is worth: the app currently returns the SAME number for both, proving it is blind to source.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses have exempt pensions (KPERS + federal civil service): fully exempt under KS law, engine taxes the full household income (defect 2 of 2, both spouses qualify)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14 enumerates both KPERS annuities and 'Federal Civil Service Retirement or Disability Fund payments and any other amounts received as retirement benefits from employment by the federal government or for service in the United States Armed Forces including Thrift Savings Plans' as fully subtractable, without a per-taxpayer or household cap (exemptionAttribution is household-wide in this app's model and there is no dollar limit in KS law for either category). Arithmetic: $25,000 KPERS + $25,000 federal civil service = $50,000, all fully exempt, leaving $0 state taxable income and $0.00 tax.

scenarios.name: MFJ, one spouse's KPERS pension is exempt and the other spouse's private pension is not: only one spouse's income qualifies (COMBINED case -- entangles both KS defects; will not go green from either fix alone, see knownDefect.summary)
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14 (KPERS annuities exempt) and the absence of any private-pension entry on that same enumerated list (private pensions remain fully taxable). Arithmetic: $25,000 KPERS is fully exempt; $25,000 private pension is fully taxable. $50,000 total minus $8,240 MFJ standard deduction minus $25,000 KPERS exclusion minus $18,320 MFJ personal exemption = $50,000 - 8,240 - 25,000 - 18,320 = -$1,560, floored at $0, so tax is $0.00 (the personal exemption plus the KPERS exclusion together exceed what remains of the private spouse's $25,000 after the standard deduction).

scenarios.name: OUT-OF-STATE GUARD, do not simplify away: single filer, a CALIFORNIA public pension held by a Kansas resident, fully taxable -- the case that proves a Kansas rule exempting ownStateOrLocal does NOT also exempt otherStateOrLocal
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14 'Retirement benefits specifically exempt from Kansas Income Tax'. Line A14 is a CLOSED list of named Kansas public plans and named federal plans (KPERS, Kansas Police and Firemen's, Kansas Teachers', Kansas Highway Patrol, Kansas Justices and Judges, Board of Public Utilities, Regents/Washburn University, certain Kansas first-class-city pensions, Overland Park Police/Fire, plus Federal Civil Service Retirement/Disability Fund, U.S. Armed Forces retirement including Thrift Savings Plans, and U.S. Railroad Retirement Board plans -- the full enumeration is quoted in the private-pension case above). A DIFFERENT state's public retirement system, e.g. the California Public Employees' Retirement System, is on none of those categories: it is neither a Kansas plan nor a federal plan, so no A14 subtraction is available and the pension stays in federal AGI, fully taxable, exactly as a private-employer pension does. This case deliberately mirrors New York's 'An out-of-state public pension: capped' guard, which exists for the same reason in the opposite direction. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: Kansas's KPERS cases in this file are labelled 'ownStateOrLocal' (Phase 5b Task 1 added the case, Task 2 re-labelled onto it). Without this case, a Kansas perSourceExemptions rule that wrongly listed 'otherStateOrLocal' among its matchSources -- the label those same KPERS rows carried BEFORE Task 2 -- would turn every KPERS case green while silently exempting this California pension too, and nothing in the fixture set would notice. Inputs are deliberately identical to the private-pension contrast case above (single, age 68, $40,000 defined-benefit pension, $40,000 federal AGI) so the ONLY difference between the three age-68 single cases is planSource, which is the axis under test. Arithmetic, identical to that private-pension case: $40,000 minus $3,605 single standard deduction minus $9,160 single personal exemption = $27,235 taxable. Kansas single brackets: $23,000 x 5.2% = $1,196.00, plus ($27,235 - $23,000) = $4,235 x 5.58% = $236.313. Total $1,432.313, rounded $1,432.31. There is no knownDefect block here and there must never be one: today's engine ships no perSourceExemptions for Kansas and so already taxes this pension in full, which is the CORRECT answer, and it must remain correct after Task 3 writes the Kansas rule.

scenarios.name: UNESTABLISHED-JURISDICTION GUARD, do not simplify away: single filer, a government pension whose employing jurisdiction was never established, fully taxable -- the case that proves a Kansas rule exempting ownStateOrLocal does NOT also exempt governmentUnspecified
scenarios.source: 2025 Individual Income Tax Booklet (ip25.pdf), page 12, Schedule S Instructions, Line A14 'Retirement benefits specifically exempt from Kansas Income Tax'. Line A14 is a CLOSED list of NAMED Kansas public plans and NAMED federal plans (the full enumeration is quoted in the private-pension case above). A pension known only to come from 'a government employer', with no jurisdiction established, is on none of those named categories: naming a plan is what puts it on the list, so an unidentified government plan has no A14 subtraction available and stays in federal AGI, fully taxable, exactly as a private-employer pension does. Kansas grants no residual exemption for government pensions in general, so nothing else can reach this income either. THIS IS ALSO A CODEBASE INVARIANT, not only a Kansas one: PlanSource.governmentUnspecified's own doc comment states that 'no rule may match this case as though it were a specific jurisdiction', and PerSourceExemptionRule.matches enforces it structurally, since a rule that names specific sources can only be satisfied by containment. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: the out-of-state guard immediately above defends ONE of the two ways a Kansas rule could over-match, otherStateOrLocal. It does not defend the other. A Kansas rule written with an EMPTY matchSources ('any source'), or one that listed governmentUnspecified outright, would turn every KPERS case green AND silently exempt this pension too, and before this case existed nothing in the fixture set would have noticed. Inputs are deliberately identical to the private-pension contrast case and the out-of-state guard (single, age 68, $40,000 defined-benefit pension, $40,000 federal AGI) so the ONLY difference across the four age-68 single cases is planSource, which is the axis under test. Arithmetic, identical to those cases: $40,000 minus $3,605 single standard deduction minus $9,160 single personal exemption = $27,235 taxable. Kansas single brackets: $23,000 x 5.2% = $1,196.00, plus ($27,235 - $23,000) = $4,235 x 5.58% = $236.313. Total $1,432.313, rounded $1,432.31. There is no knownDefect block here and there must never be one: the Kansas rule added in Phase 5b Task 3 names four specific sources and governmentUnspecified is not among them, so the engine taxes this pension in full, which is the CORRECT answer.
